clue.text: Just the opposite to quick profit

definitions.text: Just the opposite to quick profit

parts.words: Just the opposite to quick profit
parts.note: 'quick' in its old sense means living, so the opposite of a live gain is a lifeless setback, a total failure

explanation.surface: A remark about an investment that, far from paying off fast, went badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' looks like 'fast', but it is the old word for alive, as in 'the quick and the dead'; its opposite is dead, and the opposite of profit is loss.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete write-off, a venture with no return at all, is the opposite of living gain.

clue.text: Issued odd reason for scrapping

indicators.note: odd suggests something strange or irregular, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone issued a strange excuse for throwing something away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' rearranges ISSUED.
explanation.definitionFit: Neglect and lack of use are why worn-out equipment is eventually thrown away.

clue.text: Could Midas have been described as one ?

definitions.text: Could Midas have been described as one ?

parts.words: Could Midas have been described as one ?
parts.note: King Midas turned everything he touched into gold, the goal of a medieval experimenter

explanation.surface: A question about how to describe the mythical king with the golden touch.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth King Midas turned whatever he touched into gold, which is just what medieval experimenters tried to do with base metals.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval experimenter sought to turn base metals into gold.

clue.text: It's reached at the end of a flight

definitions.text: It's reached at the end of a flight

parts.words: It's reached at the end of a flight
parts.note: a flight is both an air journey and a set of stairs, and both end in the same way

explanation.surface: The moment an aircraft touches down.
explanation.walkthrough: The plane suggests touchdown, but a flight of stairs also ends at a level platform, so the word fits both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the touchdown of an aircraft and the platform at the top of a staircase.

clue.text: It's difficult when so badly scared

explanation.surface: A remark that things become hard when one is terrified.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff means hard or demanding, as in a stiff test; 'scared stiff' means terrified.

clue.text: Bark causes a conspirator to change sex

indicators.note: turning a Latin masculine name ending into the feminine one, so the -us ending is swapped for -a

parts.note: Cassius was one of the conspirators who killed Julius Caesar

explanation.surface: A tree's bark somehow linked to one of Caesar's assassins becoming a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin masculine names end in -US and feminine ones in -A, so 'to change sex' swaps the US of CASSIUS for A.
explanation.definitionFit: The aromatic bark of a cinnamon-like tree is sold under this name as a spice.

clue.text: One entitled to an army coat ?

definitions.text: One entitled to an army coat ?

parts.words: One entitled to an army coat ?
parts.note: 'army coat' suggests a soldier's tunic, but it reads as a coat of arms, which only certain people may bear

explanation.surface: A question about who has the right to wear military dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army coat' looks like a soldier's greatcoat; read it as a coat of arms, and the person entitled to it is a heraldic bearer.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry, a person entitled to bear a coat of arms.

clue.text: " My hat !" the old soldier might have said

definitions.text: " My hat !" the old soldier might have said

parts.words: " My hat !" the old soldier might have said
parts.note: 'My hat!' is an exclamation of surprise, but a soldier could also say it pointing at his tall military cap

explanation.surface: A veteran exclaiming in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My hat!' is an old exclamation of surprise; taken literally, an old soldier naming his headgear would name a tall peaked military cap with a plume.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall cylindrical military cap with a peak and plume, worn by infantry in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: After the Accounts examination I get on with the hearing

indicators.note: the following pieces come after the first one in the answer, placed behind it

parts.note: an audit is the official examination of accounts
on means getting on, as in being on stage

explanation.surface: Once the accounts have been checked, I deal with the court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' looks like a court case, but it is a performer's trial; 'After' signals that the pieces following come behind the accounts check, and 'get on' is being on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial performance in which an actor or singer is heard by those casting a role.

clue.text: Exclusively Sassenach ?

parts.note: Sassenach is the Scots word for an English person, so 'exclusively English' means with no Scots present

explanation.surface: A question whether something is purely English.
explanation.walkthrough: Sassenach is Scots for an Englishman; somewhere wholly English is free of any Scot, which is also the phrase for escaping without punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting away entirely unpunished, here read as without any Scots present.

clue.text: His authority seems momentary

parts.note: a 'second' is also a moment of time, so a deputy's rank sounds like command lasting a moment

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone's power is fleeting.
explanation.walkthrough: The deputy's title begins with 'second', which also means a brief moment, so his command sounds as if it lasts only an instant.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy officer holds the rank just below the chief, taking charge when the leader is absent.

clue.text: She precedes half the rabble in an official capacity

indicators.note: the first word is placed before the next piece in the answer, so it comes first

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the first of the two equal halves of the word for the rabble is kept

parts.note: riff-raff means the rabble, the disreputable mob

explanation.surface: A woman marches ahead of a rowdy crowd while performing some public duty.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for the rabble divides into two equal halves, and 'half' keeps the front one; 'precedes' puts the woman first.
explanation.definitionFit: A county or town officer charged with keeping the peace and carrying out court orders.

clue.text: An example of drawing craft

parts.note: 'drawing' reads as sketching skill, but here means pulling, and 'craft' means a vessel

explanation.surface: A specimen of an artist's sketching skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing craft' looks like artistic technique; read 'drawing' as hauling and 'craft' as a boat and you have a small vessel that tows ships.
explanation.definitionFit: A small powerful harbour vessel that pulls larger ships into and out of port.

clue.text: Odd number, grammatically

explanation.surface: A grammarian's remark about an odd number.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd means strange or peculiar; in grammar the number denoting just one, as opposed to plural.

clue.text: A Greek who had little, to say for himself

definitions.text: A Greek who had little, to say for himself

parts.words: A Greek who had little, to say for himself
parts.note: the Spartans of Laconia were famous for terse speech, which gave English its word for brevity

explanation.surface: A taciturn Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: Spartans, from the region of Laconia, were famous for terse speech; English 'laconic' comes from them.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Laconia, the region of ancient Sparta, whose people were famously brief in speech.

clue.text: Ten to one perhaps-the end of Nelson ?

indicators.note: only the closing part of the admiral's first name is kept, with its opening letters dropped

parts.note: Admiral Lord Nelson's first name was Horatio

explanation.surface: Betting odds of ten to one against something, and the death of Admiral Nelson at Trafalgar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The end of Nelson' looks like his death at Trafalgar; it is the end of his first name, HORATIO with HO removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten to one is an example of a proportion expressed between two quantities.

clue.text: His examination results make things go to pot

definitions.text: His examination results make things go to pot

parts.words: His examination results make things go to pot
parts.note: 'go to pot' means fall apart, but here the leaves he grades go into the pot for brewing

explanation.surface: A man whose test results make everything collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to pot' means fall apart; literally, the leaves this expert passes go into the pot, the teapot, for brewing.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert who samples brews to grade and blend leaf for the trade.

clue.text: A bird in uniform

parts.note: a woman or a prisoner wearing uniform is the one inside it, the person filling the garment

explanation.surface: A woman in uniform, such as a servicewoman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is slang for a young woman (or a prisoner); whoever is inside a uniform is the one filling it.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever fills a garment, room or post is the person residing in it.

clue.text: Where to see a bird on the water

indicators.note: in a down answer one piece sits on top of the other, so the first comes first

parts.note: a swan is a large white water bird
the sea is the open water

explanation.surface: A place to watch a swan floating on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts SWAN above SEA; the whole clue also describes the Welsh port, a city on the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A Welsh coastal city, a place answering the question 'Where?'.

clue.text: One whose activities are always above-board

definitions.text: One whose activities are always above-board

parts.words: One whose activities are always above-board
parts.note: 'above-board' usually means honest, but read literally it means moving about on top of a board

explanation.surface: Praise for a thoroughly honest person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Above-board' means honest and open, but taken literally a game piece's whole life is spent on top of a board of sixty-four squares.
explanation.definitionFit: A playing piece such as a pawn, knight or bishop always stays on the chequered board.

clue.text: Refuse to give old Bob the dregs

parts.note: a bob was the old British shilling, abbreviated s
ullage is the dregs or sediment left in a cask

explanation.surface: Declining to hand an old man called Bob the last of the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun, rubbish; a bob was slang for a shilling, the pre-decimal British coin written s.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste matter and sewage, filth and rubbish.

clue.text: The third is a questionable procedure

definitions.text: The third is a questionable procedure

parts.words: The third is a questionable procedure
parts.note: 'questionable' means dubious but also involving questions; the third kind is harsh police interrogation

explanation.surface: Criticism of a third step in a process as dubious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Questionable' means dubious, and also full of questions; the 'third' of this word is harsh interrogation by police.
explanation.definitionFit: A step on a scale; the third such step is severe interrogation.

clue.text: At least it won't run people down

definitions.text: At least it won't run people down

parts.words: At least it won't run people down
parts.note: 'run down' sounds like knocking people over, but here means carrying them away from the capital

explanation.surface: A grudging compliment about something that at least won't knock pedestrians over.
explanation.walkthrough: In British railway usage you go 'up' to London and 'down' from it; a train heading towards the capital carries nobody down, in either sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway service travelling towards the main terminus, especially London, as opposed to one leaving it.

clue.text: Palatine sense ?

parts.note: 'palatine' is an old title for a count, but here it means of the palate, the roof of the mouth

explanation.surface: A question about a count palatine's good judgement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palatine' suggests a count palatine, a noble; here it means of the palate, and the sense of the palate is the one we eat with.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the five senses, perceiving flavour through the tongue and palate.

clue.text: Distance along a motorway, by a wild eagle

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's first major motorway, written M I

indicators.note: a wild bird's letters run loose and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Measuring how far along a motorway a wild eagle has flown.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 runs from London to Yorkshire; its name, read as M and I, comes first, and 'wild' rearranges EAGLE into LEAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A count of miles covered, the length travelled by a vehicle.

clue.text: In a few words, what's. Tom up to ?

indicators.note: in a down answer, going up means the name is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A request for a brief explanation of what Tom is doing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' reads the name from the bottom upwards; 'In a few words' describes a short guiding phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A short phrase summing up a guiding principle in a handful of words.

clue.text: Head-support

parts.note: a cushion or neck brace is suggested, but 'head' means a headmaster and 'support' his staff

explanation.surface: A pillow or headrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head-support' looks like a cushion; the head is a school's headmaster, and the support is the teacher under him.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolteacher working under the headmaster, helping run the school.

clue.text: The banjoist had no up-port in Greece

indicators.note: the two words are lacking a piece, so that piece is taken away

parts.note: a joist is a supporting beam in a floor or roof

explanation.surface: A musician playing in Greece without any backing band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' is split across a line on the page; the joist is a beam, taken from THE BANJOIST to leave THE BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Thebes, the ancient city in Greece, is a person from that place.

clue.text: It might indicate a good standard of horticulture

definitions.text: It might indicate a good standard of horticulture

parts.words: It might indicate a good standard of horticulture
parts.note: 'standard' reads as a level of quality, but gardeners use it for a plant trained on a single tall stem

explanation.surface: A sign that a garden is kept to a high level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' seems to mean a level of quality; to a gardener it is a shrub grown on a bare upright stem, and roses are often grown this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A rose bush trained on a single upright stem is called a standard rose.
